opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's honestly a little bit dizzying. For most of my career, building a good math benchmark was a serious project. You'd need a group of people with real expertise sitting down for weeks or months, coming up with problems that are hard but not impossible, checking that the answers are correct and unambiguous, and making sure the problems aren't already floating around on the internet. It was slow, careful, human work.

Now you can sit down with one of these models and, in a matter of minutes, get a set of problems that, at first glance, look like they came out of that process. My first reaction is excitement, because it shows how much mathematical fluency these systems have. Generating a good problem is in some ways harder than solving one. You need taste. You need to know where the difficulty lives.

But I think the right attitude is excitement mixed with healthy skepticism. "Looks like a benchmark" and "is a good benchmark" are different things. You still need to verify that the problems are well-posed, that the answers are right, that there isn't some silly shortcut that makes them trivial. So the human role shifts. You spend less time on raw production and more on curation, judgment, and verification.

The bigger point for me is what this says about where we are. If the models can produce, in minutes, the kinds of tests we used to spend months building to measure them, then evaluation has to evolve too. We'll increasingly measure these systems on open-ended work: real research questions, problems where we don't already know the answer. That's the frontier I find most exciting, moving from AI that passes our tests to AI that helps us discover new things.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark creation used to take weeks or months, while a model can now generate problems in minutes, clearly communicating the time compression.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, it's honestly a bit surreal. I remember the first time I tried it, I didn't expect much. I just asked the model to produce a set of problems at the level of a graduate qualifying exam in analysis, with solutions, and to vary the difficulty. And a few minutes later I had something that, frankly, would have taken me a weekend to put together when I was a student, and probably longer to get right.

But I want to be careful about what that actually means, because there are two very different things going on. One is the speed, which is impressive but in some sense the least interesting part. The other is the question of whether what you get is actually a good benchmark, and that's where I think the experience is really instructive.

A benchmark is only as valuable as the thing it measures. If I generate a thousand problems in minutes, and the model that generated them can also solve them, have I learned anything? Probably not much. So the way I've come to use these tools is less "give me a benchmark" and more "let's have a conversation about what would be hard." I'll say, here's a problem, make a variant where the obvious approach fails. Or, take this theorem and find the version where the hypothesis is just slightly too weak. And the model is remarkably good at that kind of adversarial brainstorming. It's like having a very well-read collaborator who has seen every textbook exercise ever written and can remix them on demand.

What I find genuinely new is that the bottleneck has moved. It used to be that writing the problems was the expensive part. Now the expensive part is the human judgment: looking at the output and asking, is this actually testing understanding, or is it testing pattern matching? Is this contaminated, in the sense that it's basically a known result with the numbers changed? And that judgment, I think, still requires someone who really knows the mathematics.

So I'd describe the experience as humbling and energizing at the same time. Humbling because a lot of what I used to think of as skilled work turns out to be automatable. Energizing because it frees you up to think about the harder question, which is: what does it mean to really understand something, and how would we even know if a machine did?

r001.rationale: The candidate says the model produced a set of exam-level math problems in a few minutes, work that would have taken a weekend to put together before.

What excites me is how quickly you can go from an idea to something concrete that you can inspect, criticize, and improve.
